title: Qualities That Make a Character
theme: Traits and motives of characters in stories
objectives: I can explain what ten words say about how a character thinks, acts, and treats others.
I can use clues in a story to choose the best trait word for a character.
I can use the endings -ous, -ive, -able, and -ish to understand describing words.
I can write about two characters using exact trait words and proof from their actions.
rationale: Grade 3 students named basic traits such as brave and timid. Grade 4 asks them to back up a trait with evidence and to see motive and effort behind it. The ten words sort into working toward goals (ambitious, industrious, capable, dependable), treating others (selfish, cooperative, sympathetic, outgoing), and making choices (sensible, adventurous). Four of the words end in common suffixes, which opens the year's word-part work without needing a full morphology lesson. These words return in any story or biography where students must support a claim about a person.

words.def: Wanting very much to reach a big goal.
words.ex: Ambitious Tara set a goal to read one hundred books before summer.
words.ex2: The mayor's ambitious plan would plant ten thousand trees in one year.
words.nonExample: A student who never sets a goal and drifts along is not ambitious.

apps.academic: In biographies, an ambitious person works for a big goal, such as a cure or a record.
apps.spoken: I'm ambitious this year: I want to finish every book in the series.
apps.writing: Use ambitious to show that a character wants more than an easy win.

cloze.s: The ___ young chef dreamed of owning three restaurants before she turned thirty.

cloze2.s: Building a working rocket from scrap in one month was an ___ project for the science club.

misuse.s: The ambitious student had no goals and never wanted to try anything.
misuse.why: Ambitious means wanting to reach big goals; this student wants nothing.

visual.alt: An arrow in a target below a tall mountain peak.

words.def: Always ready to do what you promised.
words.ex: Dependable Marcus fed the class fish every morning, even on rainy days.
words.ex2: Our dependable old bus has not missed a day of school this year.
words.nonExample: A friend who forgets plans and never shows up is not dependable.

apps.academic: A dependable source gives the same correct facts every time you check it.
apps.spoken: You can count on me; I'm dependable.
apps.writing: Use dependable for a character whose promises can be trusted.

cloze.s: Because Jada was ___, her mom let her walk the dog alone, knowing she would come straight home.

cloze2.s: Our neighbor is so ___ that we hand him our house key whenever the family travels.

misuse.s: Sam is dependable, so nobody was surprised when he forgot his promise again.
misuse.why: A dependable person keeps promises; forgetting them again is the opposite.

visual.alt: A calendar with a check mark next to a handshake.

words.def: Having the skill to do something well.
words.ex: Even as a small child, Ines was capable of tying her own shoes.
words.ex2: The capable nurse stayed calm and solved the problem in minutes.
words.nonExample: A beginner who has never swum is not yet capable of crossing the lake.

apps.academic: Teachers say a student is capable of a task when the student has the skills it needs.
apps.spoken: I think I'm capable of doing this by myself.
apps.writing: Use capable to show a character who has the skill, not just the wish, to succeed.

cloze.s: The ___ electrician fixed the broken wiring in ten minutes while the rest of us watched.

cloze2.s: After years in the kitchen, Tomas was ___ of cooking a whole dinner for his family.

misuse.s: The capable mechanic could not fix anything and did not know what a wrench was.
misuse.why: Capable means having skill; someone who cannot fix anything lacks that skill.

visual.alt: A toolbox with a thumbs-up beside it.

words.def: Eager to try new or exciting things.
words.ex: The adventurous twins climbed to the highest branch of the old oak.
words.ex2: My uncle is adventurous at dinner and orders foods he has never tasted.
words.nonExample: A child who refuses to try anything new is not adventurous.

morph.note: The final e of adventure is dropped before -ous.

apps.academic: Explorers in history were adventurous people who traveled to unknown places.
apps.spoken: I'm feeling adventurous today; let's take a new path home.
apps.writing: Use adventurous to show a character who runs toward the unknown.

cloze.s: The ___ explorer smiled and stepped into the dark cave, eager to see what waited inside.

cloze2.s: Feeling ___, Lucia signed up to try surfing, rock climbing, and kayaking on the same trip.

misuse.s: The adventurous camper refused every new activity and stayed in the tent all week.
misuse.why: Adventurous means eager to try new things; refusing everything is the opposite.

visual.alt: A compass beside a person riding a wave on a surfboard.

words.def: Caring only about what you want, not about others.
words.ex: Selfish Rico ate the last slice of pizza without asking if anyone else wanted it.
words.ex2: It was selfish of the driver to take up two parking spaces.
words.nonExample: Sharing your lunch with a hungry friend is not selfish.

apps.academic: In a story, a selfish choice often hurts other characters and causes a problem.
apps.spoken: That was selfish of me; I should have shared.
apps.writing: Use selfish to show a character who puts his or her own wants first.

cloze.s: The ___ boy grabbed all the markers and left none for his group, though three classmates were waiting.

cloze2.s: Keeping the whole bag of popcorn while her friends watched was ___ of Maya.

misuse.s: Giving half of her lunch to a hungry classmate was the most selfish thing she did that day.
misuse.why: Selfish means caring only about yourself; sharing food is the opposite.

visual.alt: A child hugging a plate of cookies while others look on.

words.def: Showing good judgment; making choices that make sense.
words.ex: It was sensible to wear boots on the muddy trail.
words.ex2: The sensible shopper checked the price before putting anything in the cart.
words.nonExample: Wearing sandals in a snowstorm is not a sensible choice.

apps.academic: A sensible plan for an experiment lists the steps in the order they must happen.
apps.spoken: The sensible thing to do is ask for help.
apps.writing: Use sensible to praise a choice that a careful person would make.

cloze.s: Packing an umbrella was ___ because dark clouds were rolling in from the west.

cloze2.s: A ___ plan for the long hike included plenty of water and a map.

misuse.s: The sensible boy ate nothing but candy all week because it tasted good.
misuse.why: A sensible person makes wise choices; living on candy is not wise.

visual.alt: An umbrella above a person who is thinking.

words.def: Willing to work together with others.
words.ex: The cooperative group divided the jobs so everyone had a turn.
words.ex2: Our dog was cooperative at the vet and sat still for the shots.
words.nonExample: A teammate who argues about every plan and will not help is not cooperative.

morph.note: The final e of operate is dropped before -ive.

apps.academic: A cooperative group shares materials and listens to each member's ideas.
apps.spoken: Let's be cooperative and take turns.
apps.writing: Use cooperative to show characters solving a problem together.

cloze.s: The ___ players passed the ball to teammates instead of keeping it, and the team scored five goals.

cloze2.s: The nurse said Jin was ___, because he followed each step and let her finish the exam.

misuse.s: The cooperative team member refused to share the materials and worked alone.
misuse.why: Cooperative means working together; refusing to share is the opposite.

visual.alt: Two hands fitting puzzle pieces together.

words.def: Showing that you care about someone else's trouble or sadness.
words.ex: The sympathetic neighbor brought soup when Lila had the flu.
words.ex2: Mr. Lee gave a sympathetic nod when the boy said he had lost his dog.
words.nonExample: Laughing at someone who just fell down is not sympathetic.

apps.academic: A sympathetic reader feels what a character feels when the character has bad luck.
apps.spoken: I'm sorry that happened; I feel sympathetic.
apps.writing: Use sympathetic for a character who comforts someone who is hurting.

cloze.s: The ___ teacher listened quietly and said she was sorry that Ben's pet fish had died.

cloze2.s: A ___ friend sits beside you when you are sad instead of telling you to cheer up.

misuse.s: She was sympathetic to Dan's pain, so she laughed at him and walked away.
misuse.why: A sympathetic person cares about someone's pain; laughing at it does not show care.

visual.alt: A person hugging a friend who is crying.

words.def: Working hard and steadily at a job.
words.ex: Industrious ants carry food to the nest all day long.
words.ex2: The industrious students finished raking the yard before lunch.
words.nonExample: A person who naps while others work is not industrious.

morph.note: The y of industry changes to i before -ous.

apps.academic: Pioneers had to be industrious because every meal and every home took hours of work.
apps.spoken: I was industrious today and finished all my chores.
apps.writing: Use industrious to describe steady effort over time.

cloze.s: The ___ bees worked from dawn to dusk, carrying pollen back to the hive without a rest.

cloze2.s: Thanks to ___ students who raked every leaf, the school yard was clean by noon.

misuse.s: The industrious farmer slept all day while weeds took over the field.
misuse.why: An industrious person works hard; sleeping all day is not hard work.

visual.alt: A bee flying toward a jar of honey.

words.def: Friendly and happy to talk with new people.
words.ex: Outgoing Priya introduced herself to every new student on the first day.
words.ex2: My outgoing grandfather chats with everyone he meets at the park.
words.nonExample: A student who hides in a corner and avoids talking is not outgoing.

apps.academic: A character who is outgoing may start conversations that move the story along.
apps.spoken: She's so outgoing that she talks to everyone.
apps.writing: Use outgoing to show a character who welcomes other people.

cloze.s: The ___ new girl said hello to everyone at the lunch table and asked about each person's pet.

cloze2.s: Because Theo is so ___, he made three friends before the bus reached school.

misuse.s: The outgoing boy hid behind his mother and would not speak to anyone.
misuse.why: An outgoing person likes meeting people; hiding from everyone is the opposite.

visual.alt: A smiling child waving at a group.

passage.title: The Garden Behind Room 12
paras: Room 12 wanted a garden behind the school, but the plot was only hard, dry dirt. Sofia was ambitious. She wanted rows of beans, tomatoes, and sunflowers by June, so she wrote a long plan on the board.

The work was heavy, and each student found a job. Luis was industrious, and he dug for an hour without a break. Mina was outgoing, so she talked to the owner of the hardware store until he gave the class free seeds. Dev was the most dependable of all because he watered the plants every morning, even on cold days. Jin was adventurous and planted a tomato that nobody in the school had ever tasted.

Then trouble started. Carter was selfish and kept the best shovel for himself. "Mine," he said, and sat on the fence. Ms. Brooks was sympathetic when he admitted that he felt left out, but she asked him to share.

Rosa made a sensible suggestion: a chart that gave everyone a turn with each tool. Soon the whole class became cooperative. Carter even found out that he was capable of carrying three heavy buckets of water at once.
By June, the beans climbed the fence and the sunflowers grew taller than Sofia. The class had grown more than vegetables.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, the word "industrious" most nearly means
qs.why: Luis dug for an hour without a break, which shows steady hard work.

qs.q: Why does the author call Dev "the most dependable of all"?
choices: He could dig faster than anyone.
He did his job every morning, even when it was hard.
qs.why: Watering every morning, even on cold days, shows he could be counted on.

qs.q: Why does Ms. Brooks ask Carter to share the shovel?
choices: She wants him to leave the club.
She wants everyone to have a fair turn.
She does not like the fence.
qs.why: Carter kept the best tool for himself, so sharing makes the work fair for the class.

qs.q: Which detail best shows that Sofia was ambitious?
choices: She talked to the hardware store owner.
She wrote a long plan for beans, tomatoes, and sunflowers by June.
qs.why: A big goal with a plan shows she wanted to achieve a lot.

qs.q: Which sentence tells the main idea of the passage?
choices: Hardware stores should give away seeds.
Carter is the best gardener in the class.
A class can reach a big goal when everyone shares the work and the tools.
qs.why: The students succeed after they stop acting alone and start working together.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten trait words, prove each one with a character's actions, notice the suffixes -ous, -ive, -able, and -ish, and write about how people in a group act.

notes.va.ambitious.adj: Ambitious is about wanting a big goal, not about being bossy. Ask students to name the goal behind each ambitious person.
notes.va.dependable.adj: Show the parts depend + able. Have students finish: You can depend on a dependable person to ___.
notes.va.capable.adj: Capable is about skill. Contrast it with ambitious: a person can want a goal and still need practice to be capable of it.
notes.va.adventurous.adj: Adventure + -ous with the final e dropped. Ask whether adventurous is the same as careless; it is about trying new things.
notes.va.selfish.adj: Self + -ish. Students often say selfish for any person who says no. Ask whether the person ignored others' needs.
notes.va.sensible.adj: Sensible means wise and practical. Do not confuse it with sensitive; use a picture of a person choosing boots for snow.
notes.va.cooperative.adj: Co- means together. Use a human chain or puzzle task to act out the word before students write.
notes.va.sympathetic.adj: A confusable partner is sympathy versus agreement: a sympathetic person cares, but need not agree. Model a sympathetic sentence starter such as I'm sorry that ___.
notes.va.industrious.adj: Industry + -ous with y changing to i. Contrast with busy: an industrious person gets useful work done.
notes.va.outgoing.adj: Outgoing is friendly and sociable. Point out that quiet students can be kind and capable; it is not a better or worse trait.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'The text says Carter kept the best shovel for himself. He is only thinking about what he wants, so selfish fits. I can prove it with the shovel. Then Rosa makes a chart so everyone gets a turn, and the class works together, so cooperative fits the group.'
